video_title: The Market's Best Buying Opportunities Feel the Worst
gist: Morgan Stanley's Andrew Slimmon argues the late-2026 selloff is Fed-driven PE compression (22x to under 17x forward) plus an unwind of crowded AI positions, not a dot-com-style bubble, because earnings keep beating and valuations are reasonable. He cites 2028 consensus EPS of $501 (~13x), positive post-midterm seasonality, and his drawdown 'sticky note rule' to argue for buying tech and financials now.

insights.claim: Slimmon says the 2026 S&P 500 story is strong upside earnings surprise offset by more than five turns of forward-PE compression, from 22x at the start of the year to just under 17x.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: The selloff has come from the multiple, not earnings; if the multiple stabilizes, earnings growth goes straight into price.
insights.quote: the market started the year at 22 times forward earnings. And we're now, you know, as of today, just under 17 times

insights.claim: Slimmon pays attention to earnings surprise versus expectations, not absolute earnings growth, because he thinks the market already prices consensus growth accurately.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Position around whether earnings come in above or below consensus, not around headline growth rates.
insights.quote: I'm not a a believer in the earnings growth. What I'm a believer in is earnings surprise.

insights.claim: Slimmon says multiples compressed because rates rose and the Fed pivoted from neutral to hiking, which naturally makes investors pay less for each dollar of earnings.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Fed policy direction is the main driver of the multiple right now; watch the hike path more closely than the earnings tape.

insights.claim: The 2027 S&P 500 consensus EPS is $429 and rising every week, and the 2028 consensus is $501, which puts the index at about 13 and change times 2028 earnings. Slimmon calls that an extreme undervaluation unless the estimates turn out too high.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: By mid-2027 the market will be pricing off 2028 EPS; keep tracking revisions to the $501 number as the main bull/bear test.
insights.quote: the market's trading at on 13 and change times that number. Now, two things could happen. Either that number turns out to be too high, which no evidence of that yet, or I think that's an extreme undervaluation

insights.claim: Slimmon says the biggest valuation error investors make is assuming the forward-PE denominator (the consensus estimate) is accurate. Stocks that looked expensive often turn out cheap once actual earnings come in above estimates.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Judge a stock's valuation using expected estimate revisions, not the current consensus E.
insights.quote: They look at PEs and they assume the denominator is accurate.

insights.claim: Slimmon's top risk for the market is that Fed hiking cycles almost always run longer and include more hikes than Wall Street's 'comfort number' of two to four. The current expectation is one hike in February and two more next year.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Be ready for more PE compression if the Fed has to hike beyond the three moves the market expects to reach its 2% inflation target.
insights.quote: The reality is most of the time it's a lot more than that.

insights.claim: In both the 2015 and 2022 hiking cycles the market bottomed at about 15x forward earnings. The difference was that earnings fell in 2022, while in 2015 earnings held and stocks did fine in 2016-2017 even as the Fed kept hiking.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: At about 16-17x with earnings still rising, the setup looks more like 2015 than 2022; a fall in earnings would be the signal it is turning into 2022.

insights.claim: Slimmon says the current inflation surge is driven by commodities, mainly oil, unlike the 2022 surge driven by money sent to consumers. Oil, copper, softs and grains are now falling, and 2-year inflation breakevens are back near 2%.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Falling commodity prices and breakevens near 2% could let the Fed stop hiking sooner, which would be a positive catalyst for multiples.
insights.quote: Copper is down a lot. It's plunging.

insights.claim: Slimmon notes that the bull market is entering its fifth year, yet investors are unusually anxious, much of it driven by politics. That is why the multiple has lagged the earnings boom, and he expects real euphoria to show up before this cycle ends.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Missing euphoria argues the bull market has more room to run despite its age; watch for euphoria, not age, as the top signal.
insights.quote: Ultimately, bull markets die on euphoria

insights.claim: Investors pulled more money out of equities from October 2022 to October 2023 than in any period before, even as the market rallied off a 25% bear-market low.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Heavy retail outflows near a bottom are a contrarian buy signal, and the pattern repeats.

insights.claim: Based on historical analysis, buying when the S&P is down 10% does not improve the 12-month return over the 9-10% long-run average. Returns improve at -15%, more at -20%, and investing on the day the market is down 25% has averaged a 21% 12-month return. That figure matched exactly from the October 2022 low.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Scale buying into drawdowns at the -15/-20/-25% levels instead of buying routine 10% dips.
insights.quote: If you invest the day the market's down 25 %, your 12 month return goes from 9 to 10 % to 21 %

insights.claim: Slimmon keeps a 'sticky note rule' on his desk that forces him to add money at -15%, -20% and -25%. He followed it in 2022 despite feeling like 'an idiot', and says those trades made a lot of money.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Write down drawdown triggers ahead of time; mechanical rules beat in-the-moment emotion, and the same rules apply to trimming in booms.

insights.claim: Faber compares drawdowns to an inverse Richter scale, where each extra 10% decline feels 100 times worse. He thinks investor behavior breaks down at about -20%, which is why written guardrails matter.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Expect forced and emotional selling to speed up past -20%; that is when pre-committed buying pays off most.
insights.quote: every 10% down is not 10% worse it's a it's a 100 times worse. And the inflection to me seems to always really happen at minus 20

insights.claim: Slimmon points out that the market usually has a 10% correction every year to year and a half, and there hasn't been one since the tariff tantrum, so he sees the current correction as overdue rather than the end of the cycle.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Treat the current pullback as a normal mid-cycle correction.

themes.theme: AI selloff is crowding, not a bubble

insights.claim: Slimmon says bubbles burst for three reasons: extreme PEs, overly optimistic earnings estimates, or crowding. He argues today's AI/semis selloff only meets the crowding test, because memory stocks trade at very low single-digit PEs and hyperscalers are not expensive.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: A crowding-driven unwind with intact fundamentals is a buying opportunity, not a 2000-style top.
insights.quote: These PEs the memory stocks are trading at you know very low single digits.

insights.claim: Slimmon contrasts today with the late 1990s: the largest tech stocks then traded at 80-100x earnings, while today's hyperscalers trade at reasonable valuations. He says the market got anxious because they shifted cash from buybacks to data-center capex.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Multiple compression on rising capex can reverse once cloud revenue growth shows up.

insights.claim: Slimmon says the internet buildout ended when supply caught up with demand (fiber, routers), but AI still shows scarcity: memory chips and compute are short and advanced chip makers say demand is sold out. He reads that as early-cycle AI.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: The signal to exit AI infrastructure is supply catching up with demand, not price volatility; track sold-out backlogs and memory pricing.
insights.quote: my core belief is that we're early cycle on AI

insights.claim: Slimmon thinks the Nasdaq/QQQ selloff is a liquidation of crowded positions by both individuals and institutions, not a change in fundamentals. That makes AI and tech names a better buy now than they were a month and a half ago.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Add to tech and AI on liquidation-driven weakness, though forced selling can push prices further than valuation suggests.
insights.quote: valuation gets tossed out the window when people need to liquidate

insights.claim: Slimmon does not expect political pushback to stop the data-center buildout. Financially strapped municipalities will find it hard to turn hyperscalers away, though projects may slow and companies will have to give back to communities instead of seeking tax breaks.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Regulatory headlines slow the AI capex story but don't end it; fear of capex 'ending' is overdone.

insights.claim: Slimmon is cautious on software vendors whose specialized outside-vendor services can be replaced by in-house AI tools, while seeing AI overall as a cost-saving tool like the internet.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Underweight point-solution software and data vendors exposed to AI substitution; this is not a call against all software.

insights.claim: Slimmon thinks the current flood of large IPOs adds supply that is pulling selling into other stocks. He sees that as a short-term effect, unlike the late 1990s when daily IPOs had no revenue or earnings.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Watch IPO lockup expirations as a short-term supply overhang, not a sign of a bubble top.

insights.claim: Slimmon treats industrial cyclicals as a better read on the economy than economists' forecasts. He says they show the data-center buildout has been a boom for many industrial companies.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Use industrial earnings calls to check the health of the AI capex cycle and the economy.

insights.claim: Slimmon says growth stocks are not expensive today, unlike 2021 when growth was the priciest it had been outside the dot-com peak, so he doesn't expect a growth-stock bloodbath. His strategies are tilting more toward growth.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Lean into growth on the drawdown instead of hiding in value or defensives.

insights.claim: Slimmon sees consumer staples at a 25-year valuation high while tech trades at a steep discount to staples. He reads the recent rotation into defensives as liquidity flows, not a durable signal.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Rich staples versus cheaper tech sets up a reversal; fade the defensive rotation.
insights.quote: what am I doing owning toothpaste and diapers?

insights.claim: From the end of 2009 through 2024, Europe compounded about 5% a year, Japan 6% and the S&P 500 14%. Slimmon says cheap non-US valuations were a trap because their earnings never came through.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Valuation alone is not a reason to own non-US markets; you need earnings delivery.

insights.claim: Since Q1 2025 Europe and Japan have outperformed or kept pace with the US because their earnings revisions turned positive after 15 years of falling estimates. Slimmon points to European banks as the example.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Low PE plus positive revisions is the best mix; non-US exposure, especially European banks, now has fundamental support.

insights.claim: Slimmon says positive earnings revisions tend to persist and are one of the best predictors of long-term stock returns, better than growth or valuation. Misses rarely turn out to be one-offs because both management and buy-rated analysts have an incentive to downplay them.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Screen for positive estimate revisions and be skeptical of 'one bad quarter' explanations.
insights.quote: Companies with positive earnings revisions outpace companies with negative revisions over time.

insights.claim: Slimmon notes that data shows concentrated managers who control risk outperform diversified ones, but most investors fire underperforming managers within 12-18 months. On that rule, investors could never have held Warren Buffett or Charlie Munger.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Concentrated, high-active-share strategies need a longer evaluation horizon than investors usually allow.

insights.claim: Slimmon notes that the second year of the four-year presidential cycle (2026) is historically the lowest-returning, most volatile year. Since 1950, though, the S&P 500 has been up in the 6- and 12-month windows after every midterm, 19 out of 19 times.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Seasonality strongly favors adding equities into the post-midterm window that starts now.
insights.quote: the period six months after the midterm and 12 months after the midterm, uh the market has been up every time

insights.claim: In 17 of 19 midterms the opposing party gained seats. Slimmon thinks the resulting gridlock, like the post-'blue wave' DC gridlock now, lets investors stop focusing on Washington and get back to fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Gridlock is market-friendly; political anxiety is a poor reason to sell.

insights.claim: Faber notes that the coming January is historically the best single month of the cycle in the last 100 years, especially for small caps.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Small caps look attractive tactically going into January 2027.

insights.claim: Slimmon thinks late November 2026 will look like a good entry point into beaten-down tech and financials.
insights.speaker: Andrew Slimmon
insights.so_what: Accumulate tech and financials into year-end weakness.
insights.quote: I think financials have been creamed too.
